answer.rationale: Constraints prune the option set before evidence does. rollback_release is barred by compliance (the security patch must stay), and regional_failover directly threatens the primary objective of not losing customer writes — shifting regions mid-peak with heavy in-flight writes risks exactly the loss we are told to avoid, so memory_b2's clean March recovery (a latency-degradation case, not a write-heavy peak) does not transfer. That leaves relieving pressure on the write path. memory_b5 is the closest structural match: taking read load off the primary recovered transactional write latency same-day, which is the mechanism we need now. I spend verification on memory_b5 because my whole plan rests on it — I need the original record to confirm the load profile was comparable (peak write traffic, not an off-hours dashboard spike) and that relief came from replica routing rather than a co-occurring change. I spend the second pull on memory_b3 because add_capacity is my fallback: the archived record should show whether headroom was provisioned days ahead of the retail peak (in which case it cannot help within this incident window) or provisioned live. Scale is a small guarded test, per memory_b6's lesson that staged cohorts surface regressions within an hour — I route a bounded slice of report/analytics queries first and watch p99 and replica lag rather than flipping all reads at peak. Two honest gaps I am not papering over: the true cause may be the un-revertable release itself, in which case read offload buys headroom without fixing anything and I will need the next window for a circuit breaker per memory_b4; and routing reads to replicas serves staler data to settlement reporting at daily peak, which is a real downstream correctness risk for any process that reads-then-writes on those numbers. I am flagging that rather than treating replica routing as free.
